​Heavy fog and mist are currently impairing visibility across the City of Joburg. Please follow these precautions to stay safe on the roads:

​Reduce Speed: Adjust your driving to account for limited visibility.

​Keep Your Distance: Increase your following gap to allow for sudden stops.

​Use Headlights: Keep your low-beam headlights on (avoid high beams as they reflect off the fog).

​Stay Alert: Be cautious of pedestrians and slower-moving vehicles.

​Drive safely and arrive at your destination alive. 🚔💨

data.raw_text:
Four years ago Meta tried to launch a global currency and got destroyed by regulators on live television.

Yesterday they quietly launched stablecoin payments anyway.

No press conference. No white paper. No Senate hearing. Just a new page on Meta's website saying creators can now receive payouts in $USDC on Solana and Polygon.

That's it. That's the whole move.

And it's a masterclass in how you actually get crypto into a billion-person product after the regulator burned your first attempt to the ground.

Here's what happened in 2019 for anyone who needs the context.

Meta announced Libra a global stablecoin backed by a basket of currencies, run by a consortium of 28 companies including Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, and Uber. 

The pitch was simple: send money across borders as easily as sending a text. The reaction from Washington was not simple. Congressional hearings. Regulatory threats. 

One by one every major partner quietly exited the consortium. By 2022, the project was dead and buried under the name Diem.

The lesson Meta took from that wasn't "crypto is too risky."

The lesson was "don't announce a global currency. Just build the rails."

➝ So what did they actually build this time?

No new token. No proprietary blockchain. No basket of currencies. 

They plugged into existing infrastructure $USDC, which is already regulated, already institutional, already used by Circle which just filed for an IPO. 

They chose Solana and Polygon, two chains that already have the throughput to handle Meta-scale volume. 

The whole thing is framed as a creator payout feature, not a financial system.

That framing is deliberate. A creator payout feature doesn't need a Senate hearing. It needs a product manager and a compliance sign-off.

But zoom out for a second and look at what this actually is.

Meta has 3.27 billion daily active users across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. 

The creator economy on those platforms generates billions in transactions annually. 

A meaningful percentage of those creators are in markets where traditional banking is expensive, slow, or structurally inaccessible Southeast Asia, Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa.

$USDC payouts on Solana to a creator in the Philippines or Nigeria isn't a product feature. 

It's financial infrastructure for markets that legacy banking never properly served.

➝ And here's the connection nobody is making right now.

The GENIUS Act the first federal stablecoin law passed the Senate last week. It creates a regulatory framework that explicitly legitimizes $USDC-style stablecoins under federal oversight. 

Meta didn't launch this by accident this week. They've been waiting for exactly this regulatory window.

Libra failed because it tried to become the regulatory framework before the regulatory framework existed. 

This launch succeeds or at least survives because it's operating inside a framework that Congress just built.

The CLARITY Act is still pending. But stablecoins now have their lane.

One more thing worth noting.

Solana got the nod here alongside Polygon. That matters. SoFi already launched enterprise banking on Solana this month. 

Israel's first regulated stablecoin launched on Solana. Now Meta's creator payments run on Solana.

The institutional use case for Solana isn't coming. It's already happening on the 12.8 second finality chain, before Alpenglow even ships.

Meta didn't announce a revolution. They just quietly plugged 3.27 billion users into onchain rails.

That's actually more dangerous to traditional payments infrastructure than anything Libra ever proposed.
